name: Morgan Sindall Group plc
executive_summary: Morgan Sindall Group plc is a UK partnerships, fit-out and construction-services group that has compounded earnings through a decentralised, cash-generative model: FY 2025 revenue reached £5,018.6m with adjusted profit before tax up 35% to £233m, and a secured workload of £11,972.2m (secured plus preferred-bidder work £19.1bn). The quantitative screen rates the shares a strong buy; `screening_snapshot.json` is not in this pack, so P/E, yield and model-pass detail cannot be verified here. Filing evidence supports a net-cash compounder rather than a distressed deep-value name: average daily net cash was £374.2m in FY 2024 and the FY 2025 dividend rose 20% to 158p. The debate is whether Fit Out’s surge and public/regulated construction visibility justify the screen, or whether UK housing cyclicality, contract risk and missing interims, screen metrics and 2025 cash figures mean the market is right to be cautious.
investment_thesis:
For a value investor the stated strong-buy screen is coherent with a high-quality, capital-light cash engine funding longer-cycle partnerships, not with a broken balance sheet. The screen file itself is missing, so this overlay uses only the stated signal, not reconstructed multiples.

What the filings do show is a multi-year quality run. Group revenue rose from £3,213m in FY 2021 to £5,018.6m in FY 2025; adjusted profit before tax rose from £127.7m to £233m. Management cites an 18% CAGR in adjusted profit before tax over ten years. Average daily net cash stayed substantial throughout (£291.4m in FY 2021, £256.3m in FY 2022, £281.7m in FY 2023, £374.2m in FY 2024). The dividend rose from 92.0p to 158p over the same span, inside a stated cover range of 2.0–2.5 times. Secured workload expanded from £8,614m to £11,972.2m, and FY 2025 closed with a record combined order book and preferred-bidder pipeline of £19.1bn.

The business mix matches that cash-and-quality profile. Fit Out (Overbury/Morgan Lovell) is described as market leader, capital-light and the principal cash generator; Construction, Infrastructure and Property Services are also cash-generative, with Construction and Infrastructure around 77% public and regulated in FY 2023. Partnership Housing (Lovell) and Mixed Use Partnerships (Muse, formerly Urban Regeneration) absorb capital to win long-dated public-sector schemes. Management’s own capital-allocation framework, introduced in 2021, prioritises balance-sheet strength, a downturn buffer, regeneration investment and an attractive dividend — the same attributes a value screen typically rewards.

The quality caveat the screen cannot see is concentration and cyclicality. Fit Out revenue jumped from £1,300.3m in FY 2024 to £1,784m in FY 2025, so a large share of the latest earnings step-up sits in commercial office fit-out. Mixed Use Partnerships revenue fell to £52m from £90.5m, underscoring lumpy development recognition. Private housing remains subdued. Without the screen snapshot, cheapness versus this franchise is unverified in-pack; the filings confirm business quality more clearly than they confirm valuation.
financial_review:
Primary source: Companies House body extracts under `filings/bodies/`. `filings_index.json` (regime `uk_rns`) labels all five items `period: other` (annual 0, interim 0). In substance they are five consecutive group annual reports (FY 2021–FY 2025, filed May 2022–May 2026). There are no consolidated half-year results, no RNS trading-update bodies, and no parent-company interim in the index. `financials_annual.json` is not in the pack; no Yahoo fallback was used. Extracts are partial OCR of strategic-report sections: full consolidated balance sheets, cash-flow statements, note 28 APM reconciliations, and going-concern/viability wording are not in the bodies. All figures below are from those extracts.

Coverage gap. No filing labelled `annual` or `interim`. The FY 2025 report refers to a trading update released on 12 February 2026; that RNS is not in this pack. FY 2025 statutory profit before tax and average daily net cash are not readable in the OCR highlights box (comparatives £171.9m and £374.2m are). Adjusted operating profit is rendered as “£225./m”; treated here as £225.7m, consistent with the FY 2024 comparative of £162.6m printed beside it.

Annual results — FY 2021 (Annual Report 2021, Companies House 16 May 2022).
Revenue £3,213m (2020: £3,034m); adjusted operating profit £131.3m (2020: £68.5m); operating margin 4.1% (2020: 2.3%); statutory operating profit £129.8m; adjusted profit before tax £127.7m; statutory profit before tax £126.2m; average daily net cash £291.4m (2020: £180.7m); secured workload £8,614m; total dividend 92.0p (cover 2.46 times). Construction & Infrastructure operating profit £58.1m on revenue £1,520m (margin 3.8%). Fit Out revenue grew 14% to £795m, profit £44.2m at a 5.6% margin. Partnership Housing revenue £572m, operating profit £33.2m, margin 5.8%, return on capital 21%.

Annual results — FY 2022 (Annual Report 2022, Companies House 20 May 2023).
Another record year against a harder backdrop. Revenue £3,612m (+12%); adjusted operating profit £139.2m; statutory operating profit £88.3m; adjusted profit before tax £136.2m (+7%); statutory profit before tax £85.3m; average daily net cash £256m (later reports: £256.3m); secured workload £8,459m; total dividend 101.0p (cover 2.36 times). The statutory/adjusted gap is largely an exceptional building-safety charge of £48.9m (£5.5m Partnership Housing, £43.4m Urban Regeneration) after signing the Developers Pledge and reviewing Building Safety Fund grant reimbursement. Q4 private-home sales on mixed-tenure sites slowed; Urban Regeneration saw cost-inflation pressure on some scheme returns, described as not material overall.

Annual results — FY 2023 (Annual Report 2023, Companies House 18 April 2024).
Revenue £4,117.7m (+14%); adjusted operating profit £141.3m (+2%); adjusted operating margin 3.4% (2022: 3.9%); statutory operating profit £140.6m; adjusted profit before tax £144.6m (+6%); statutory profit before tax £143.9m (+69%), “driven mainly by an exceptional building safety credit of £2.2m compared to a charge of £48.9m in 2022”; average daily net cash £281.7m; secured workload £8,920.2m; total dividend 114p (cover 2.2 times). Divisional revenue: Construction £966.6m, Infrastructure £886.7m, Fit Out £1,105.2m, Property Services £185.2m, Partnership Housing £837.5m, Urban Regeneration £185.3m. Property Services recorded a loss after cost and labour inflation. Partnership Housing capital employed averaged £255m (2018: £115m); Urban Regeneration averaged £99m (2018: £109m). Around 77% of Construction and Infrastructure work was in public and regulated sectors.

Annual results — FY 2024 (Annual Report 2024, Companies House 12 May 2025).
Record year again. Revenue £4,546.2m; adjusted operating profit £162.6m; statutory operating profit £162.0m; adjusted profit before tax £172.5m; statutory profit before tax £171.9m; average daily net cash £374.2m; secured workload £11,419.3m; total dividend 131.5p. At the half year the Group restyled itself as the “partnerships, fit out and construction services group”; Urban Regeneration was renamed Mixed Use Partnerships. Divisional revenue: Partnership Housing £861.2m, Mixed Use Partnerships £90.5m, Fit Out £1,300.3m, Construction £1,044.1m, Infrastructure £1,047.0m, Property Services £223.2m. Mixed Use Partnerships’ order book grew from £1,825.6m to £4,084.9m, with £2.36bn of development agreements signed. Medium-term targets were upgraded for four of six divisions. Outlook language: on track for 2025 “in line with our current expectations.”

Annual results — FY 2025 (Annual Report 2025, Companies House 14 May 2026; Chief Executive’s statement).
Revenue £5,018.6m; adjusted operating profit £225.7m (OCR); statutory operating profit £224.9m; adjusted profit before tax £233m (+35%); secured workload £11,972.2m; secured plus preferred-bidder work £19.1bn (OCR “179%”; 17.9% year-on-year is the only reading consistent with an £11.4bn–£12.0bn secured book). Total dividend 158p (+20%). Statutory profit before tax and average daily net cash for 2025 are not in the extract. Divisional revenue: Fit Out £1,784m, Construction £1,159m, Infrastructure £935m, Partnership Housing £903m, Property Services £212m, Mixed Use Partnerships £52m. Mixed Use Partnerships converted eight sizeable preferred-bidder schemes to signed development agreements and won eight new preferred-developer appointments. Partnership Housing secured Cardiff, Vale of Glamorgan and Barnet schemes for a collective 3,000 homes and preferred-developer status on Birmingham’s Druids Heath regeneration (around 3,500 homes). Medium-term targets were raised for Mixed Use Partnerships and Infrastructure. Headcount is described as more than 8,500 (FY 2024: more than 8,000). Outlook: positive despite housing headwinds; on track for 2026 “in line with revised expectations” in the 12 February 2026 trading update (not in this pack).

Trend. Five consecutive record adjusted-PBT years, with the sharpest step-up in FY 2025 as Fit Out scaled and group adjusted operating margin recovered from 3.4% (FY 2023) to about 4.5% on the OCR operating-profit figure. Cash generation funded both a rising dividend and partnership investment. Offsets: Mixed Use Partnerships’ reported revenue is lumpy; Infrastructure revenue fell in FY 2025 versus FY 2024; Property Services remains the operational weak spot in earlier years; private housing is still described as subdued. Group interim trading after 31 December 2025 cannot be assessed from this index.
risks_and_flags:
Cyclical construction and housing. The Group is UK-centric. Private-home sales on mixed-tenure sites slowed from late 2022; FY 2025 still cites “current headwinds in the housing market” and only a gradual recovery as rates ease. Mixed Use Partnerships revenue is inherently lumpy (£185.3m / £90.5m / £52m over FY 2023–FY 2025). Fit Out now dominates group revenue; a downturn in commercial office refurbishment would hit cash generation that funds partnerships.

Contract, supply-chain and operational risk. FY 2023 flagged supplier liquidity stress and a Property Services loss from cost and labour inflation. Construction policy is to let revenue fall to protect margin “if we hit challenging times,” which is disciplined but implies earnings can recede. The FY 2025 extract notes Partnership Housing stepping in where original contractors had gone into administration — industry distress around the Group, not a Group insolvency. Principal-risk pages are listed in contents (FY 2025 pages 48–54) but the risk-register text is not in the bodies.

Regulatory / building safety. FY 2022 recognised a £48.9m exceptional provision under the Developers Pledge and Building Safety Act; FY 2023 took a £2.2m credit. Later extracts mention the Building Safety Act as a legal obligation but do not update the provision. Residual cladding/fire-safety cash outflows are therefore a live but unquantified item in this pack.

Governance and key person. John Morgan remains Chief Executive across all five reports. Peter Harrison became chair in 2025 after Michael Findlay retired in July 2025 following nine years. No CEO succession detail appears in the extracts. Culture and decentralisation are presented as strengths; they also concentrate execution risk in divisional management (Property Services in 2023 is the exhibit).

Liquidity, leverage, covenants, going concern. Contents list “Going concern and viability statement” in each annual report; the extracted bodies do not include the statement text, facility size, covenant tests or year-end net cash for FY 2025. Average daily net cash through FY 2024 argues against a liquidity stress, but that is not a substitute for the missing statement. Treat covenants and going concern as a data gap, not a clearance.

Pension. No defined-benefit surplus, deficit or IAS 19 figures appear in the extracted bodies.

Competitive / public-policy. Affordable-housing and infrastructure volumes depend on grant, RP balance sheets and the pace of the June 2025 Spending Review commitments (National Housing Bank £16bn of new public investment; Affordable Homes Programme £39bn over ten years; 10-year rent settlement of inflation plus 1%). Slippage in those programmes would slow Partnership Housing and Mixed Use Partnerships more than Fit Out.

Accounting. Results are presented on an adjusted basis with a note 28 reconciliation that is not in the extracts. The FY 2022 building-safety exceptional is the main distortion; subsequent years’ adjusted and statutory profit are close.

RiskTags: cyclical, competitive, regulatory, key_person, other
news_highlights:
`news_manifest.json` is missing. Coverage in this pack is thin: no yfinance or Google News RSS file, and the filings index contains only Companies House accounts. Material items below are narrated inside the annual reports, not third-party headlines.

- Chair succession: Peter Harrison appointed; Michael Findlay retired from the Board in July 2025 after nine years (FY 2025 Chief Executive’s statement).
- Identity and structure: at H1 2024 the Group adopted the description “partnerships, fit out and construction services group”; Urban Regeneration was renamed Mixed Use Partnerships (FY 2024 report).
- Strategy / order book: £2.36bn of Mixed Use development agreements in 2024; eight conversions from preferred bidder plus eight new preferred-developer wins in 2025, including Druids Heath with Birmingham City Council (c. 3,500 homes) and Cardiff / Vale of Glamorgan / Barnet (c. 3,000 homes collectively).
- Policy backdrop cited in the FY 2025 report: June 2025 Spending Review and Autumn Budget; National Housing Bank; £39bn Affordable Homes Programme; inflation-plus-1% ten-year rent settlement.
- Trading update dated 12 February 2026, used as the reference for “revised expectations” for 2026 — the announcement itself is not in the source pack.
- No M&A, profit warning, or regulatory enforcement action is documented in these bodies. Flag: there is no structured year of headlines with which to cross-check management changes after the FY 2025 report, short interest, or post-balance-sheet trading.
research_rationale: FY 2021–FY 2025 filings confirm a net-cash, dividend-paying earnings compounder that supports rather than contradicts the strong-buy screen, but missing screen metrics, group interims, 2025 cash/statutory profit and news coverage mean deep research only partially confirms the case.
